extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors and readers of philosophical/literary works
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on how to read philosophical/literary works profitably and how to decide whether to become (or how to behave as) an author. Covers criteria for choosing what to read, how to read (whole vs. excerpt), self-examination before authorship, and cautions about hasty publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presume yourself ignorant of a writer's understanding until you understand his ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: Until you understand a writer's ignorance, presume yourself ignorant of his understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge presents this as a golden rule for perusing philosophical works: attempt first to discern the grounds and limits of the writer's knowledge (their 'ignorance') — e.g., trace the causes that acted on a fanatic's mind to explain his visions without accusing him of intentional falsehood. If you can follow these traces with tranquil certainty you 'understand' the writer; if baffled in explaining a great author's obscurities (as with parts of Plato) you may conclude 'ignorant of his understanding.' The rule is illustrated with examples (a religious fanatic and Plato) and is intended to correct rash dismissals and to foster charitable, analytic reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read whole connectedly or omit the chapter
rubrics_metrics.description: Either pass over the following chapter altogether, or read the whole connectedly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On 'delicate subjects' the author warns that taking a part from the organic whole will produce a deformed or monstrous impression — a faithful display of main ideas separated from the forms that clothe them becomes a 'skeleton' that may alarm and deter. Thus do not rely on isolated extracts; read the chapter (or work) in its contiguous context to appreciate meaning and avoid misjudgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not demand absolute removal of prejudices, but aim for unprejudiced reading
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader is not required to strip his mind of all prejudices nor to keep prior systems entirely out of view; though an unprejudiced mind is desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge admits his request to be read with an unprejudiced mind is idealistic and not strictly enforceable. He counsels against insisting that readers abandon all previous systems, while still urging charitable and careful attention. The point: seek openness but be realistic about prior commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-screening criterion for whether the chapter is for you
rubrics_metrics.description: If a man receives as fundamental facts (indemonstrable and incapable of further analysis) the general notions of matter, spirit, soul, body, action, passiveness, time, space, cause and effect, consciousness, perception, memory and habit, and feels his mind at rest about them, the chapter was not written for him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a practical test offered to conjecture in advance whether reading will be profitable or infuriating: the chapter targets readers who do not take those basic categories as final. If you already feel fully at rest about these ultimate notions and analyze everything into them, you will likely find the chapter irrelevant or unhelpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogue scruples and test motives before choosing authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Before deciding against or for authorship, catalogue your scruples, reduce them to distinct intelligible form, and ascertain whether other influences may be at work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge advises strict self-examination: ensure scruples are genuine, that you have read fundamental works on the subject with a docile mind, and that your heart and mind are open to the qualities of illustrious predecessors. He recommends finding older contemporaries who had similar scruples and acted on them to learn from their later judgments (some regretted leaving the 'high road' for an erroneous labyrinth). Time spent in such delay can be beneficial to judgment and temperance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid authorship too early or immoderately
rubrics_metrics.description: With the neatest possible solicitude avoid authorship. Too early or immoderately employed, it makes the head waste and the heart empty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted from Herder and endorsed by Coleridge: reading only to print produces bad habits — 'he, who sends away through the pen and the press every thought the moment it occurs, will in a short time have sent all away, and will become a mere journeyman of the printing-office.' Practical counsel: do not rush to publish every passing thought; cultivate restraint and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read for understanding, not merely to print
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who reads only to print probably reads amiss; avoid reading solely as preparation for immediate publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complementing the previous rule: if your reading is instrumental (only to supply copy), your reading and writing quality will suffer. The text recommends deeper, reflective reading where ideas are allowed to re-circulate within the mind rather than be immediately expelled into print.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoughts must be re-circulated and re-secreted for intellectual vigor
rubrics_metrics.description: What medical physiologists affirm of certain secretions applies equally to our thoughts; they too must be taken up again into the circulation, and be again and again re-secreted in order to ensure a healthful vigor, both to the mind and to its intellectual offspring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge's own addition: creative and intellectual health requires internal reworking and maturation of ideas. This counsels against immediate publication and in favor of revisitation, incubation, and reexpression of thoughts before committing them to print.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be more than a man of letters; let literature augment but not constitute you
rubrics_metrics.description: Be not merely a man of letters. Let literature be an honorable augmentation to your arms; but not constitute the coat, or fill the escutcheon!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical life and career counsel: combine literary pursuits with other occupations or roles. Coleridge argues that other professions supply social sympathy, steadiness, prudence, and domestic happiness that pure authorship often lacks. He recommends maintaining broader social engagement and identities beyond being solely an author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not imagine authorship is less beset by temptations to dishonesty
rubrics_metrics.description: The trade of authorship besets its members with temptations as insidious as the Church, the law, or commerce; it is not a profession free from temptations to dishonesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge warns against romanticizing authorship as morally superior or safer. Aspiring writers should recognize ethical challenges in literary life and cultivate honesty and honor as in any other reputable profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: On judging philosophical works, value unifying, perspective-giving synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: A true philosophy explains and collects the fragments of truth scattered through systems apparently the most incongruous; it shows regularity and coincidence of all parts in one central perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge suggests that a good philosophical work reconciles doctrines, finding elements of truth in many sects and bringing them into a coherent whole. Readers and critics should look for works that collect and reconcile rather than merely add new jargon or isolated propositions.
